name: Nasal testosterone (Natesto)

lead: Natesto is a prescription testosterone gel given through the nose for men with low testosterone. People on TRT discuss it because small studies suggest it may keep sperm production and gonadotropins more intact than other testosterone forms.

The appearance link is the usual TRT one: restored testosterone supports muscle and lower fat. Trials in hypogonadal men report normalised testosterone, and several small studies report preserved semen parameters. A 90-day trial of 306 hypogonadal men found the nasal gel normalised androgen levels, with extensions to one year. These studies are in medical patients, not cosmetic users.

paras: It is short-acting, so it is applied several times a day under a prescriber's direction. It suits people who want an alternative to skin gels or injections and who care about fertility.

As with other testosterone products, reported concerns include raised hematocrit, blood pressure monitoring, acne, and prostate and cardiovascular questions. It is a controlled prescription drug and is banned in competitive sport.

web.title: Natesto (testosterone) nasal gel prescribing information (FDA label)
FDA approves Trimel's Natesto nasal gel to treat adult males with low testosterone

angle.text: Natesto is a prescription nasal testosterone for diagnosed low T, popular in TRT circles because small studies suggest it may keep sperm production more intact. The looks link is the usual TRT one, more muscle and less fat, studied in hypogonadal men.

lead: Natesto is a prescription testosterone nasal gel used for testosterone replacement in men with hypogonadism (clinically low testosterone). It is supplied as a metered pump that delivers the gel into the nostrils, and Wikipedia lists it as the intranasal testosterone product among testosterone formulations [1][2].

For appearance, the connection runs through hormone status. Testosterone influences lean mass, body-fat distribution, energy, libido and mood, so men whose levels are restored from a deficient range may notice changes in body composition and vitality [1][3]. A phase 3 stratified analysis tracked lean body mass, mood and erectile function alongside hormone levels in men on the gel [3]. It is not a cosmetic product and is prescribed for diagnosed deficiency.

What sets it apart in muscle and hormone communities is its short-acting profile. Because it is dosed several times a day and clears quickly, several small studies report that men on it kept their LH, FSH and semen parameters, in contrast to what is typically reported with long-acting testosterone [4][5][6]. In a 90-day randomised, open-label, dose-ranging study of 306 hypogonadal men, the gel brought testosterone into the normal range for most participants, with safety extensions to one year [7].
infobox: Trimel Pharmaceuticals; US approval announced May 2014 [9]
Short-acting; several times daily under prescriber direction [7][10]

paras: Testosterone was first approved for medical use in 1939, and over the following decades was supplied as injections, patches, skin gels, pellets and oral products [1][8]. Nasal delivery was developed to offer a short-acting alternative that avoids skin contact. Trimel Pharmaceuticals announced the FDA's approval of Natesto, previously known as CompleoTRT, at the end of May 2014 and described it as the first testosterone nasal gel approved for replacement therapy in adult men [9].

In its announcement the company's chief executive said men could use the product "without worrying about the risk associated with transferring the product to women or children" [9]. This secondary-exposure point is a recurring theme in descriptions of nasal gel, since skin gels can transfer testosterone to people in close contact. The label today is held by Acerus Pharmaceuticals Corporation [10].

Natesto's labelled use is testosterone replacement in adult men with hypogonadism, meaning symptoms and repeated low morning blood testosterone readings [7][2]. The Medical Letter's 2015 review of the product noted that it raised low serum testosterone into the normal range in hypogonadal men and that whether patients would prefer it to injections every few weeks or daily skin gels remained to be determined; it also repeated the FDA's warning against using testosterone for hypogonadism due solely to aging [2].

Reviews of treatment options place nasal gel among several categories of testosterone replacement, alongside injections, skin gels, patches, pellets and oral products, and describe the choice as shaped by convenience, side-effect profile and the patient's fertility plans [11][12]. Because exogenous testosterone generally suppresses the pituitary signals that drive sperm production, fertility-minded men and clinicians have looked at short-acting options and at drugs such as clomiphene or hCG as alternatives [6][13].

Wikipedia notes that low testosterone is assessed on a morning blood sample, that the American Urological Association supports a diagnosis when total testosterone is below 300 ng/dL, and that routine screening of men without symptoms was not recommended as of 2018 [8]. Impaired muscle development, gynecomastia, reduced libido and erectile difficulty are among the described symptoms of male hypogonadism [8]. The Natesto label's pivotal study enrolled men whose morning testosterone was 300 ng/dL or below [10].

sections.h: Uses in appearance and training contexts
paras: Testosterone replacement is described as supporting libido, mood and secondary sexual characteristics, and hormone optimisation is a recurring subject in muscle-building forums [6][14]. The phase 3 analysis of Natesto reported lean body mass, mood and erectile function outcomes by baseline testosterone group [3]. All of this evidence comes from men with diagnosed deficiency rather than from healthy men seeking a cosmetic effect.

The FDA label states that Natesto is for replacement therapy in adult males with conditions associated with deficiency or absence of endogenous testosterone, including primary and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and that safety and efficacy have not been established for age-related hypogonadism [10]. Contraindications include breast carcinoma or known or suspected prostate carcinoma in men, and use by pregnant or breastfeeding women [10].

Warnings and precautions in the label cover blood pressure increases, polycythemia (hematocrit is checked before treatment, at three to six months and then annually), nasal conditions (not recommended for chronic nasal conditions or altered nasal anatomy), abuse and dependence (testosterone is a Schedule III controlled substance), and venous thromboembolism reports [10]. In the 90-day study subset described in the label, the most common adverse reactions were increased PSA (5.1%) and, at 3.8% each, headache, runny nose, nosebleed, nasal discomfort, nasopharyngitis, bronchitis, upper respiratory infection, sinusitis and nasal scabbing [10]. The label was revised in July 2025 and now carries a blood pressure increase warning [10].

The 2023 TRAVERSE trial, a randomized placebo-controlled study of 5,246 men aged 45 to 80 using a transdermal testosterone gel, found major adverse cardiac events in 7.0% of the testosterone group and 7.3% of the placebo group, meeting its noninferiority criterion; atrial fibrillation, acute kidney injury and pulmonary embolism were more frequent with testosterone [15]. The label cites TRAVERSE for its venous thromboembolism discussion, and the trial did not test the nasal formulation [10][15].

Testosterone products as a class can cause acne, breast enlargement, raised hematocrit, worsened sleep apnea and, with prolonged use, reduced sperm production, and are contraindicated in pregnancy [1]. One phase 3 analysis studied men with seasonal allergies, a group relevant to a nasally delivered product [16].

Secondary polycythemia, a rise in red-cell concentration, is a known effect of testosterone therapy. A cross-sectional comparison and a randomised trial update examined polycythemia rates in men on nasal gel versus intramuscular testosterone cypionate, framing the short half-life of the gel as relevant to that risk [17][18]. A registered phase 4 study was set up to monitor ambulatory blood pressure in men on the gel [19]. The FDA's caution about testosterone in age-related decline is cited in the product review [2]. Advantages reported in the pivotal study include ease of administration, low dose and no risk of secondary transference to partners or children, unlike skin gels [7].

The gel is delivered into the nasal cavity, and testosterone is absorbed across the nasal lining into the bloodstream, giving short-lived peaks rather than the steady levels of long-acting preparations [7][4]. Doses are taken two or three times a day in the studies, and a MY-T study analysed how symptoms guide dose adjustment by prescribers [7][20]. A small study of five healthy men looked at how intranasal use shows up in anti-doping laboratory markers [21].

The label describes administration as a metered pump delivering gel into each nostril, with no application to other parts of the body; in the 90-day study's three-times-daily group, mean day-90 testosterone was 421 ng/dL [10].

Testosterone is a controlled substance in many countries, available only by prescription in most, listed as Schedule III in the United States, and banned in competitive sport by the World Anti-Doping Agency [1].

subs.h: Use in training and hormone communities
paras: On T Nation forum threads, members describe nasal testosterone as an option that "will not shut you down" and that adds to natural production, and some mention it as a way to test how they respond to treatment [22][14]. Others note that it is more expensive than injectable testosterone and compare it with compounded nasal products [23]. A patient-preference study compared satisfaction with topical and nasal testosterone [24]. Public discussion is mostly about men who already have a clinical diagnosis.

In the 306-man dose-ranging study (mean age 54.4 years, 39 US sites), 73% of the intent-to-treat group reached the eugonadal average testosterone range at day 90, with higher percentages in the fixed twice-daily arm than in the titration arm, followed by safety extensions to one year [7].

A stratified analysis of the phase 3 data compared testosterone, LH, FSH, erectile function, mood and lean body mass across baseline-testosterone groups, and another analysis covered men with seasonal allergies [3][16]. A University of Miami single-arm trial evaluated effects on reproductive hormones, semen parameters, quality of life and sexual function, and an earlier interim report of the ongoing trial described maintained FSH, LH and semen parameters [4][5]. A registered phase 4 trial with 60 participants studied the same outcomes [25].

Small clinical series reported spermatogenesis resuming after switching from long-acting testosterone, and, in 41 men, improved libido with maintained semen parameters and reduced estradiol after switching from clomiphene [26][27]. Comparative work includes a polycythemia comparison with intramuscular testosterone and a patient-preference study against topical products [17][24][18]. A blood-pressure monitoring study in 218 men is registered [19]. Doping-marker work in five healthy men has also been published [21].

lore.intro: In T Nation and similar hormone communities, nasal testosterone is discussed mainly as a short-acting way to supplement testosterone while preserving the body's own production [22][14].
